Two awesome projects.

simslim&avdslim

Keywords: Found two projects · simslim · avdslim

So, I found these two awesome projects: simslim and avdslim.

simslim

Processes25870

Memory4.0 GB0.9 GB

Keywords: Every simulator: lots of background processes, unnecessary · memory spikes with two or three · simslim disables them · lighter simulator, easy to create, less memory

Now, by default each simulator runs with a lot of background processes that are unnecessary. This spikes up the memory very quickly when I spin up two or three simulators at the same time.

Click: the unneeded processes switch off.

simslim will disable those processes and give you a lighter version of the simulator, one that can be easily created and usually takes less memory to run.

The numbers are from simslim’s README: one simulator on an M1 Pro with 16 GB.

Cloud simulators.

Nice. Still pricey.

Keywords: Large team, one project · still a bottleneck · cloud simulators · Expo’s, two days ago, early access · nice but pricey · others building · nothing stable yet

Now, even with multiple devices we might be bottlenecked when there is a large team working on one project. That is where cloud simulators come into play.

Expo released their cloud simulator server just two days ago. I got to try it out as an early accessor. It’s nice, but still pricey though.

I think some other companies are also trying to build something along this line. Right now nothing is stable or ready to use, and even if it is, it’s costly.

Or run your own farm.

💻→📱📱📱📱

Mine is an old laptop.

Keywords: Mac mini or Studio as a mobile farm · my old laptop is the server · spin up and control the simulator from my Mac · less memory here, more in parallel

And there are other ways, obviously. If you have a Mac mini or a Studio, you can use that as a mobile farm and run the simulators from there.

I have turned my old laptop into a server. I can spin up and control a simulator from my Mac and test it there. Less memory consumption on my Mac, and more work done in parallel.

iOS apps.
Built on Linux.

Keywords: iOS app built on Linux · omarchy-apple-dev · whenever I need a build, it runs on that machine

We can now build an iOS app on Linux, thanks to this awesome project.

So whenever I need to do a build, I do it on that system.

Ship from the terminal.

$asc builds upload --ipa App.ipa

$gpc bundles upload --file app.aab

Keywords: How do we publish without Xcode? · App Store Connect CLI · grateful to the maintainer · no more App Store Connect dashboard · Android: playconsole-cli

Now, this doubt might have appeared for you: without an Apple distribution certificate, how can we publish? That is where this awesome CLI comes into play: App Store Connect CLI.

I am grateful to the maintainer each and every day that I don’t have to go through that horrible App Store Connect dashboard. I can do most of the things I need from this CLI itself.

And there is something similar for Android: playconsole-cli.

One more:
Mobile Dev.

Live devicesDevice controlLogsPerformanceProfile analysisApp storageTesting StudioNetwork conditions

Codex. Claude. T3 Code.

Keywords: Recently found · Mobile Dev plugin, Callstack · built on agent-device · works in T3 Code, Codex, Claude · I use it there · live devices, logs, performance, profiles, storage, tests

Okay, there are just so many things there. I get your feeling.

Recently I found this plugin, Mobile Dev, which is built on top of agent-device. It can be integrated with T3 Code, Codex or Claude, and I am personally using it there.

Even though T3 Code has its own device panel, this is cool and it has most things to offer: live devices beside the chat, device control, native and JavaScript logs, performance monitoring, profile analysis, app storage and a testing studio.

My workflow.

ship-builds&perf-check

Keywords: Two skills · ship-builds: build and publish from the Linux box · perf-check: runs the performance-critical pages · stores the numbers · next push must not be worse · could be CI, cost, so my Linux machine

I have a ship-builds skill, which delegates the build process to my Linux box, does all the steps, and publishes from there.

And I have another skill, perf-check. It runs all the performance-critical pages, and new pages if needed, and stores those details. When the next change or push happens, it is allowed to be pushed only if the numbers are not worse than the previous ones.

We can do this in the CI layer, but due to cost constraints I am doing this on my other Linux machine.

Our job changed in one year.

Set the agent up for success.

Keywords: One thing to take away · our job changed drastically in a year · who knows in two or three · good codebase, better systems · set the agent up for success · play with new things · keep improving the workflow

If there is one thing I would like you to take from this talk, it is this. Our jobs as developers and engineers have changed drastically from one year ago. And who knows how it will look another two to three years down the line.

As good engineers, our current job is to create a good codebase and better systems that will set the agent up for success.

I am exploring new tools and workflows all the time. I hope you take this, play with new things, improve the workflow continuously, and create a codebase in a way that will set the agents up for success.
